question: By virtue of Regulation (EU) 2023/851, which brings an end to the marketing of internal combustion engines from 2035, the European automotive industry is obliged to embark on a forced change that will put thousands of jobs at risk. In late January 2024, the German multinational Robert Bosch GmbH, the leading manufacturer of car components, announced that it would cut 1 200 jobs by 2026 owing to transition costs.

Another German company, ZF Friedrichshafen, the world leader of components in the transport industry, also announced that up to 12 000 jobs could be lost for the same reason. A study by the European Association of Automotive Suppliers found that the balance between jobs lost and gained by the transition to electricity is negative, with 275 000 jobs lost by 2040, of which up to 60 000 will be in Italy.
Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
What it will do to address the serious social problems that will arise with the transition to electric?
Whether it considers it appropriate to revise certain parts of the ‘Fit for 55’ package concerning forced conversion to electric cars?
With a view to safeguarding thousands of jobs, whether it considers it appropriate to save internal combustion engines by focusing on alternative technologies, such as biofuels?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2024) The automotive sector is undergoing a profound transformation towards zero-emission and digital mobility. Analysis shows that transport electrification alter supply chains with structural shifts in employment from traditional manufacturing towards battery production, electricity supply and related investments1.
The transition is expected to deliver a net positive impact on jobs across the economy2. Dedicated funding is available to accompany workers, businesses and regions in this transition3.

Various initiatives under the European Green Deal and its Fit for 55 package support the necessary workforce adaptation through job-to-job mobility, upskilling and reskilling, alongside facilitating the creation of new employment opportunities.

Such initiatives include the Council Recommendation on ensuring a fair transition towards climate neutrality4, providing guidance to Member States on comprehensive just transition policies. In addition, skills development is also supported by the EU Skills Alliance and its Pact5, including the Automotive Skills Alliance6.

Moreover, the Commission published the Transition pathway for the EU mobility industrial ecosystem7 in January 2024, a co-creation process with stakeholders that includes 112 actions to support long-term resilience and competitiveness of this ecosystem. Renewable fuels including sustainable biofuels will play an important role in the energy transition.

However, in a view to deliver the decarbonisation of the European economy in an affordable way, they will play a particularly important role in hard to decarbonise sectors such as maritime, aviation and industry while decarbonisation of road transport will rely to a large extent on electrification.
